articles.title: Serbia's Parliament To Meet For First Time Since Opposition's Landslide Election Victory
articles.summary: Three weeks after winning a landslide election victory, Serbia's Student List opposition movement gets to flex its new political muscles as the country's parliament meets for the first time on November 17.
articles.body: BELGRADE -- Three weeks after winning a landslide election victory , Serbia's Student List opposition movement gets to flex its new political muscles as the country's parliament meets for the first time on November 17. The initial focus is electing a new speaker but the gathering of lawmakers also sets the clock ticking on electing a new government, a process that must be completed within 90 days. The Student List has 140 seats in the 250-seat parliament, putting it in the driver's seat after 14 years dominated by former President Aleksandar Vucic . But the leaderless movement has yet to say who it will nominate for speaker, prime minister, or other top jobs. Who's In Charge? The Faces Of Serbia's Student-Backed Political Movement Milan Bogunovic, a former veterinary surgeon who was elected for the Student List, told RFE/RL's Balkan Service that the main task at hand was rolling back the authoritarian system established by the Vucic years. "Establishing the rule of law, ensuring respect for the law, and making the system function properly. Everything that has failed to work over the years must start working," he said. His words were echoed by his colleague Mirza Ramusovic, a 35-year-old lawyer from Novi Pazar in southwest Serbia, where the majority of the population is Bosniak. "After 14 years of political stagnation and hopelessness, we have a new opportunity to implement reforms and chart a new course for Serbia," he told RFE/RL. The Student List emerged from a student movement that spent two years leading mass anti-government protests and insisted on accountability for the collapse of the canopy at Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024, which killed 16 people. Arrests, Resignations, Repainting: Here's What's Happening In Postelection Serbia Its platform is centered on fighting corruption and organized crime, ensuring the independence of the judiciary and prosecution service, and safeguarding media freedom. It's an important role, whose holder plays a large part in setting the legislative agenda. In addition to this, the new speaker will also be acting president following Vucic's resignation in June. A new presidential election must be held by the end of the year. Until the election of a new speaker, the parliament is chaired by its oldest serving member -- in this case, 78-year-old mathematician Stojan Radenovic, elected on Vucic's United Serbia list. Vucic will lead the United Serbia faction in parliament, of which his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is the key member. The party did not respond to RFE/RL questions for this article, but Vucic has pledged it "will behave decently and responsibly" in opposition. Political scientist Dusko Radosavljevic said the SNS had never learned how to behave in a parliamentary manner. The previous majority was frequently accused of failing to respect parliamentary procedures. Over the years, neither bills nor amendments proposed by the opposition were accepted. While presiding over parliamentary sessions, former Speaker Ana Brnabic was often criticized for bias, selective application of the rules of procedure, and restricting opposition lawmakers from speaking. Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade, told RFE/RL that the character of the new parliament would be shaped by its expert composition. "The Student List is an expert-driven list, a kind of technocratic ticket, with a large number of PhDs and university professors," he said. "Citizens were clearly dissatisfied with the way experienced opposition politicians had operated." Radosavljevic said the backgrounds of the Student List legislators could also led to better laws. "When substantive legislation is debated, whether it concerns education, health care, or agriculture, there will be many people who genuinely understand those issues," he said.

articles.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
articles.body: Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements. The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin. Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said. The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 . Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest". The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights. The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc. In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean. In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda". Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants". He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration". Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants. The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role. "IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms". With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration. Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries . Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo. "Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad." The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution. The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place. According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year. In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands". Five EU countries announce plan to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda
articles.summary: In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to ​abandon the Rwanda plan.
articles.body: Five European countries have announced a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a processing centre in Rwanda as early as next year, drawing condemnation from rights groups who said it would leave vulnerable people at risk of abuse. The planned scheme, which is still being negotiated with Rwanda, would send people to a centre where the migrants could choose to return home, settle or go somewhere else where they had a right to stay, Kigali said on Monday. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands said that the plan aimed to deter more people from migrating to Europe. The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, reduce the number of asylum seekers arriving and increase deportations of migrants who are not entitled to stay. “I think this will be a game changer, making us able to confront the massive challenges with illegal migration,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. “We will break down the business model of human smugglers. We will take back control of our borders and we will remove the incentives for illegal migration.” Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, said his country would give a “second chance” to people who have no right to stay in Europe. He added that arrivals would be able “to voluntarily return to the countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society or relocate to another destination where they have the legal right to reside, according to their preference”. When asked how Kigali would ensure refugees’ human rights, Biruta said, “There will be an independent monitoring mechanism” and that it would cooperate with the United Nations’ refugee agency. Human rights groups criticised the plans, saying that EU countries could not guarantee their rights would be respected there. In a joint statement, 47 aid, trade union and rights groups urged ‌the five countries to abandon the Rwanda plan — echoing criticisms of a different migration settlement plan between Britain and Rwanda in the early 2020s. The plan “signals that Member States accept the risk of serious human rights violations against one of the most marginalized groups in society, in return for a deterrence goal that evidence clearly suggests they will not reach,” read the statement from the International Rescue Committee, the Dutch Council for Refugees and other groups. A Human Rights Watch researcher said the deal “would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad”. Germany’s interior minister said the European plan was not comparable to a scrapped 2022 deal with the United Kingdom because only those whose asylum claims are rejected will be sent to Rwanda. The UK’s Supreme Court ruled that the 2022 deal was unlawful because Rwanda was not considered a safe third country to which migrants could be sent.

Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
articles.summary: The Estonian government says Russia was behind the attempted sabotage, which the Kremlin denies.
articles.body: The Estonian government says it will shut the crossings after accusing Russia of directing an alleged sabotage attack on a drone manufacturer Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe". The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian. They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids. On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries. The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website. Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia". Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage. The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media. Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions. One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border. Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls." Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months. Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored. Australian MP Helen Haines leaves hospital after losing both legs in alleged car attack
articles.summary: The attack has sparked much soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats towards elected officials.
articles.body: An Australian lawmaker said she was "full of gratitude" as she was discharged from hospital on Monday following an alleged attack in October that resulted in her losing both legs.Independent politician Helen Haines was struck outside her office in rural Australia, suffering serious injuries that eventually led to the amputation of her legs.The attack has sparked much soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats towards elected officials.The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said the 65-year-old had been discharged four weeks after she was airlifted in for emergency treatment."I am very pleased to confirm that I have moved into the rehabilitation stage of my recovery, which will continue in Melbourne for the immediate future," she said in a statement."This is a really positive moment and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage."Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he was in regular contact with Haines and her family and wished her the best for her recovery."We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation," he said in a statement.Haines was standing near her car in the rural Australian town of Wangaratta when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on 19 October.Police have charged 43-year-old Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official.Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as cracking down on corruption and stronger climate action.

articles.title: Bahrain Says It Intercepted Iranian Attacks As Tehran Claims Strike On US Base
articles.summary: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it had targeted a US military installation.
articles.body: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed it had targeted a US military installation. The Bahraini military said its air defenses intercepted several attacks before they reached their targets, accusing Tehran of continuing its "systematic hostile approach" toward the kingdom. Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the country rejected "turning its territory into an arena for settling scores" and held Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. Iran's IRGC claimed they had launched six drones targeting a US air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, according to statements carried by Iranian state media. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities that the radar installation had been hit. Citing its journalists in Bahrain, the AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around 4 a.m. local time, followed by another series of blasts around 6:30 a.m. Sirens also sounded and Bahraini authorities issued warnings urging residents to seek shelter without specifying the source of the threat. The Interior Ministry told residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow official channels for updates. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, has been among the Gulf countries targeted by Iran during the conflict, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. The reported attack on November 15 came two days after the IRGC said it had targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain. The US military said at the time that it had intercepted two Iranian drones targeting the island, reporting no casualties or damage. Bahrain has now been targeted twice in three days, following a lull in attacks. The latest developments come amid diplomatic efforts to end the nearly nine-month conflict, which have not yet produced a breakthrough despite a broader lull in fighting. Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global oil transit route, and launched missile and drone attacks on military and civilian infrastructure across the region. US President Donald Trump has told his senior advisers in recent days that he might refrain from further attacks on Iran if Tehran and Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen avoid new provocations, according to Reuters. Trump has also said the US naval blockade of Iran would remain in place. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's military said on November 15 it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province. Armenian Opposition Slams Pashinian Government Over ‘Political Prisoners’
articles.summary: The hearings in the National Assembly were initiated by the opposition Hayastan (Armenia) alliance and attended by members of the Strong Armenia bloc, as well as political and public figures not represented in parliament.
articles.body: The hearings in the National Assembly were initiated by the opposition Hayastan (Armenia) alliance and attended by members of the Strong Armenia bloc, as well as political and public figures not represented in parliament. Speakers at the event noted that the leaders of both parliamentary blocs – former President Robert Kocharian and Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetian – as well as Gagik Tsarukian, the leader of the Prosperous Armenia Party, which fell just short of the threshold to enter parliament in the June elections, are currently imprisoned on what they described as politically motivated charges. Speaking at the session, Lilit Galstian, a lawmaker from the Hayastan faction and head of the parliamentary human rights committee, accused Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian of personally directing the persecution of political opponents from the parliament’s rostrum. As evidence, Galstian cited past warnings by Pashinian that he would send opponents to the notorious “National Security Service dungeon.” Pashinian has repeatedly denied directing any arrests, dismissing such remarks as mere political rhetoric. Civil Contract lawmakers did not attend the proceedings. Volodia Hakobian, secretary of the ruling party’s faction, told RFE/RL’s Armenian Service that his party stayed away from the event because “there are no political prisoners in Armenia.” Hakobian added that it was “ridiculous” for allies of former President Kocharian to raise the issue, hinting at what Civil Contract and its supporters assert were large-scale persecutions of opposition figures during his 1998-2008 presidency. Civil Contract’s decision to skip the session follows a move last week by the ruling majority in the parliament’s committee on state and legal issues to reject a draft opposition statement on democratic backsliding in Armenia under the Pashinian government, which also referred to the presence of political prisoners. During that committee debate, ruling party lawmaker Arman Yeghoyan dismissed the opposition’s assessments, arguing they had “nothing to do with reality.” During Monday’s hearings, Gohar Meloyan, of the Strong Armenia bloc, called for an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the in-custody death of her teammate, Arsen Gevorgian. Meloyan alleged that Gevorgian, a mayoral candidate in Stepanavan who had been arrested on vote-buying charges, died from an apparent heart attack due to a lack of proper medical care. Government officials have disputed that claim. Last week, both Justice Minister Srbuhi Galian and the head of the Penitentiary Service stated that Gevorgian had received all necessary medical treatment prior to his death. Former lawmaker Naira Zohrabian also used her address at the hearings to criticize Justice Minister Galian, who had emotionally stated last week that she and her underage child were being targeted in the wake of Gevorgian’s death. “You are a representative of a political party whose supporters harassed my child during the 2018 political upheaval by telling her that her mother had died and instructing her to go to the morgue to retrieve my body. You are a member of the team that placed coffins outside the doors of living people,” Zohrabian said. Opposition lawmaker Anna Grigorian, who chaired the session, intervened to state that children should not bear responsibility for the actions of their parents, either in 2018 or today. Among those who spoke at Monday’s hearings was the 14-year-old daughter of Aregnaz Manukian, a leading member of the opposition Mayr Hayastan party who is being prosecuted as part of a high treason case against party chairman Andranik Tevanian. After her imprisonment in July, Manukian, whom the opposition also considers a political prisoner, was barred for weeks from seeing or speaking with friends or relatives, including her daughter. Law enforcement authorities reluctantly allowed the girl to visit her mother in prison in August following an uproar from opposition and public figures.

articles.title: Public Defender submits amicus curiae brief to Constitutional Court regarding banning of political parties
articles.summary: The Office of the Public Defender of Georgia submitted an amicus curiae brief to the Constitutional Court regarding the banning of political parties, the Public Defender's Office reports. According to them, the purpose of the document is to highlight, by examining relevant standards, the key legal aspects that will assist the Court in properly assessing the submitted lawsuit on banning political parties.
articles.body: The Office of the Public Defender of Georgia submitted an amicus curiae brief to the Constitutional Court regarding the banning of political parties, the Public Defender's Office reports. According to them, the purpose of the document is to highlight, by examining relevant standards, the key legal aspects that will assist the Court in properly assessing the submitted lawsuit on banning political parties. "On September 24, members of the Parliament of Georgia submitted a constitutional lawsuit seeking to declare five opposition political parties unconstitutional and to ban them. Given that the review of such a lawsuit represents a novelty for Georgia's legal system, the Public Defender decided to submit an amicus curiae brief to the Constitutional Court of Georgia. The amicus curiae brief summarizes the relevant case law of the European Court of Human Rights regarding the scope protected by freedom of association and its lawful restriction. Thus, by examining the relevant standards, the document aims to highlight the key legal aspects that will assist the Court in properly assessing the submitted lawsuit on banning political parties," the statement notes.

articles.title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
articles.body: Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight. The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks. At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “ O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us! ” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin , the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines. UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent , which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds. Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march. UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police . West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward. Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance . The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage. Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail). Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU. Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions. But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme). Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.” The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”. Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed. There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses. The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage. And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.” On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working? In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis. Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs. A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund. It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit. I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back” ? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe? The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.” But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says. The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right , street protests , hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026 . “There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh. There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget. Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?” Tuesday | The former health and social care secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released. Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia. Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place. With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture , and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read . Poppy Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand ’s prominence. Poppy Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure. Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win , with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera. articles.title: Nikoloski: respect for the Constitutional Court shows institutional maturity
articles.summary: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski…
articles.body: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski said in his address at the fourth annual conference of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, held in Ohrid on the topic “Contemporary Challenges to the Rule of Law: The Role of Constitutional Courts.” Nikoloski stressed that the role of the Constitutional Court is particularly important in this time of rapid social, technological, and political changes. As he put it, “that is why institutions must be stable, institutions must be resilient, and institutions must survive political changes.” The independence, professionalism, and integrity of constitutional judges and of the Constitutional Court are key to fulfilling this function. The rule of law implies not only the adoption of high-quality decisions, but also their respect and implementation. The executive and legislative branches have the responsibility to create the conditions for the full implementation of the decisions of the Constitutional Court, which very often also mean a correction of certain decisions that may have been taken without sufficient analysis and without sufficiently taking all the facts into account, and sometimes even with some other intention. That is why the foundation of the Constitutional Court is precisely this — to help make corrections where corrections need to be made, Nikoloski pointed out. He noted that respect for constitutional justice is an indicator of a state’s institutional maturity and democratic responsibility. That is why we strive to respect the Constitutional Court and to give it the place it deserves in the state-legal order. The independence of the judiciary should, of course, not be understood in isolation from the other institutions, but rather as a guarantee of impartial and objective decision-making, and also as a way of improving society. Mutual control and balance among the three branches of power — and here, of course, the Constitutional Court as a separate body — play a significant role in maintaining a functional state, Nikoloski emphasized in his address before constitutional judges from the country and abroad. The Deputy Prime Minister also referred to the new challenges, such as digitalization and artificial intelligence, which on the one hand can be an advantage, but on the other hand also a threat. Of course, knowledge, experience, and the human factor remain irreplaceable, and I cannot agree with certain debates that are being conducted, that even in this area — in the area of respecting the Constitution, in the area of implementing the Constitution, and in the area of implementing and respecting the laws — we should rely on artificial intelligence. I think that is wrong, and I think it is something that we need to think about very seriously as a state and as states, because this is a broader debate, not only in our country, but I repeat, I believe that is not the path we should follow, because knowledge and personal experience are something that is irreplaceable and that no machine can do, Nikoloski said. At the closing of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, Deputy Prime Minister Nikoloski stressed that a strong state does not mean only a strong executive power, but a limited executive power, a state with strong and independent institutions, institutions that complement each other and control one another. Therefore, as a representative of the executive branch, as Deputy Prime Minister, I can say that as a Government we will do everything and we are doing everything for this system to continue to function and to be further developed, Nikoloski said.

articles.body: Russia has designated Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin as its counterpart to Georgia’s newly appointed special representative for relations with Russia, George Zurabashvili, and has established contact with the Georgian official, the Russian Foreign Ministry told the Russian newspaper Izvestia. “The appointment of Georgia’s First Deputy Foreign Minister George Zurabashvili as the Prime Minister’s special representative for relations with Russia reflects Tbilisi’s interest in maintaining and developing channels of communication with our country," Izvestia cited the Russian MFA as saying. "We welcome this. Russia has consistently advocated for building pragmatic and mutually beneficial relations with Georgia. We have established contact with George Zurabashvili," the Ministry added. 11/08/2026 - Russia’s Galuzin Reiterates Openness to ‘Further Expanding Pragmatic Ties’ with Tbilisi Zurabashvili, Georgia’s First Deputy Foreign Minister, was appointed as the Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze's Special Representative for Relations with Russia on October 21, filling a position that had remained vacant since December 2025. He was allowed to retain his current position at the Foreign Ministry, a decision that also required Georgia's parliament to adopt the respective legislative changes in October. The appointment has drawn concern among former Georgian diplomats, who warned of a “dangerous trend” and questioned whether the move could amount to de facto restoring diplomatic relations with Moscow. Kobakhidze's remarks while presenting the new Special Representative also left an impression among professional circles that Tbilisi was expanding the post’s mandate, previously limited to trade, economic, humanitarian, and cultural issues, to now also cover “the peaceful resolution of the conflict with the Russian Federation." The post of a Special Representative was established as part of the informal direct dialogue between Georgia and Russia launched in late 2012, commonly known as the Abashidze-Karasin format. Grigory Karasin, Russia's initial representative, also served as Russian Deputy Foreign Minister from 2005 to 2019. The Russian Foreign Ministry described the move as involving "the resumption of the Russian-Georgian dialogue, which was launched in 2012 and operated for nearly 10 years," considering "this mechanism, known as the 'Karasin-Abashidze format,' to be successful and useful." 02/02/2023 - Karasin-Abashidze Audio Recording Sparks Opposition Criticism Izvestia further cited the Russian MFA as saying that it views "the promotion of people-to-people contacts, the development of trade and economic cooperation, tourism, transportation links, and the implementation of cultural projects as the priority tasks of this new channel of communication." It also expressed hope that "Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s decision to appoint a special representative for relations with Russia will give the Russian-Georgian dialogue additional momentum and allow us to place bilateral cooperation on a more systematic basis." Zurabashvili replaced Giorgi Kajaia, who took up the post in March 2024 after a four-year term as Head of Georgia’s Interests Section at the Swiss Embassy in Russia, and held it until December 2025, according to Kobakhidze. Kajaia succeeded Zurab Abashidze, who served as Special Representative from 2012 and was later appointed Kobakhidze’s advisor. Refused UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal
articles.summary: Home Office plans will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety, say refugee charities Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.
articles.body: Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow immigration enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice. Currently, enforced returns for rejected claimants can only take place after a minimum notice period of five working days, which can allow people to launch other legal interventions or prepare themselves for removal. Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, condemned the change. “We must treat people with dignity. Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety,” he said. “We also need to look at the evidence of what works. The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns. If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer.” Louise Calvey, the executive director at Asylum Matters, said: “People deserve a fair chance to make their claim for help and sanctuary, but forcibly removing people from the country so they don’t get a chance to make their claims won’t fix that. “Right now, 63% of the population don’t have access to an asylum legal aid provider. What that means is people are attempting to navigate a horrendously complex and hostile system in a new country, often in a second language. In that environment, many people may not have had the proper advice in initial claims, so many who make further claims are found to have a genuine need for support. “Expelling people from the country to ensure we never get to hear their legitimate claims is nothing to be proud of – it will lead to real injustices.” Mahmood has tabled an amendment to the immigration and asylum bill that will scrap the five-day timeframe. Officials would instead be given a six-month period to remove refused asylum seekers and rejected migrants before further notice is required, the Home Office said. The changes follow a similar approach to the system that Denmark successfully operates, the Home Office has said. The number of migrants awaiting removal in Denmark was cut from more than 2,185 cases at the end of 2020 to fewer than 1,000 at the end of 2025. The UK has increased the number of removals since Labour came to power, but faces huge backlogs in asylum applications. As of 30 June 2026, 40,168 people were waiting for an initial asylum decision in the UK. The number of refused applications hit more than 90,000 in the same month, breaking previous records. There are currently exceptions to the five-day notice period for removals, such as where the removal was disrupted by the individual or was cancelled due to bad weather. In these scenarios, removal can be attempted again without further notice for 21 days. This timeframe will now be increased to six months under reforms in the bill, which returns to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading on 17 November. The bill will also introduce a new immigration appeals authority with the aim of speeding up removals and changes to how human rights and modern slavery laws are applied to asylum applications to root out what the government described as “vexatious” claims. Ministers hope the bill will bring into force proposals that will create a firm but fair asylum system, and which will reduce the pull factors driving illegal immigration. Under other reforms, the responsibility to make modern slavery decisions for children will be devolved to local safeguarding partners. This will ensure professionals who already support the child, and are closest to the child, are making the decisions for their future, the Home Office said. Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said: “This government is ramping up removals of those with no right to be here, with over 80,000 illegal migrants and foreign nationals returned since the general election. “Now we are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.”

Bosnia’s New Presidency Takes Office for 2026-2030 Term
articles.summary: The three members of Bosnia's state presidency – two of whom are women – took office on Monday following last month's elections, and will mostly be in charge of foreign policy.
articles.body: Darijana F ilipovic, Zeljka Cvijanovic and Denis Becirovic pose for a photo after their inaugural session. Photo: N1. Bosnia and Herzegovina’s newly elected tripartite presidency took office on Monday at a session in Sarajevo, with Denis Becirovic, Zeljka Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic beginning their four-year mandates. Speaking after his inauguration, Bosniak representative Becirovic, who is beginning his second consecutive term, said his priorities would include defending Bosnia’s sovereignty, protecting human rights and advancing the country’s European Union and NATO integration. He also pledged to promote equality and fight discrimination. His vision, he said, was of an economically strong, technologically developed and socially just Bosnia and Herzegovina, fully integrated into both organisations. He called for an end to divisive political rhetoric, saying political energy should be directed towards building a safer future. “People draw no benefit from populism and arguments. They want peace, security, social justice and good prospects for their children,” he said. Serb representative Cvijanovic, also beginning her second consecutive term, called on domestic politicians to take full responsibility for the country’s future rather than expect solutions from abroad. She criticised international intervention in Bosnia’s politics, arguing that decisions imposed over the previous four years had deepened political crises. She also said the domination by one constituent people over the other two was unacceptable. Croat representative Darijana Filipovic called for the presidency to show more responsibility towards voters. “From today, the question is no longer who was given trust, but what we can do with that trust,” Filipovic said. She said she would work to ensure that Croats in Bosnia felt politically represented and equal. “We are not asking for Croats to have more, and we do not accept that they have less. I believe the same rule must apply to everyone else in this country, because Bosnia and Herzegovina … must be a country in which people have equal worth,” she said. Filipovic succeeds Zeljko Komsic, who served four terms as the Croat member of the Presidency but who was widely seen as owing his place to Bosniak votes. The new Presidency is the first since the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement established the institution to include two women, Cvijanovic became the first woman to serve on the body in 2022. The three members were elected in the October 4 general elections, with the Central Election Commission confirming the results on November 3. Under the Presidency’s rules, the chairmanship rotates every eight months. Bosnia’s state presidency is responsible for foreign policy, appointing ambassadors and other representatives to international organisations and proposing the annual state budget to parliament, based on a recommendation from the Council of Ministers.

articles.title: EU Commissioner ‘Regrets’ Serb Song About Kosovo at Brussels Event
articles.summary: Following complaints, Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos expressed regret for the performance of a Serb nationalist ballad about Kosovo at an EU event in Brussels, saying it does not reflect the European bloc's position.
articles.body: European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos speaking in Brussels, 16 November 2026. Photo: EPA/Olivier Hoslet. The European Commissioner for Enlargement, Marta Kos, on Monday said she regretted that a controversial song about Kosovo was performed before the opening of the European Enlargement Forum in Brussels. “I regret the choice of the song by the musicians. It touches sensitive feelings, particularly given the history and different experiences of the communities in Kosovo,” Kos, a Slovenian diplomat, said in Brussels. “I want to stress that this song in no way reflects the position of the European Commission or myself with respect to Kosovo and history,” she added. The song,“Oj Kosovo, Kosovo”, celebrates Serbia’s claims to its former province. Its lyrics say that Kosovo “has always been ours” and vow never to give up the territory. It was performed as an instrumental version, by a Slovenian band, at a concert on Sunday, preceding Monday’s European Enlargement Forum. The choice of song was made by the performers rather than the organisers, according to Kos. Jeton Zulfaj, Kosovo’s chief negotiator with the EU, asked Kos “to explain how this happened and what measures she will take, and why Kosovo, the biggest democratic climber in the Western Balkans this decade and fully aligned with EU foreign policy and EU values, was not invited”. On X, Zulfaj called the incident “scandalous and unacceptable. An EU event on enlargement cannot give a stage to Serbian nationalism.” The Albanian Prime Minister, Edi Rama, also condemned the incident. “I don’t know if it was deliberate or ignorance but a tasteless nationalistic song was performed on the eve of this event in the contrary of everything it represents,” Rama said. Riho Terras, a European Parliament member and Kosovo rapporteur, also demanded an explanation from the European Commission and Kos. “Performing a Serbian nationalist song asserting claims over Kosovo at an EU enlargement event is an extraordinarily tactless and tasteless blunder,” he said. The author Ljubomir Manasijevic recounted in 2019 that the song was created in 1989, inspired by the celebration of the Battle of Kosovo’s 600th anniversary near Pristina, at which Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic gave a fiery speech which has been identified by some historians as marking the beginning of Yugoslavia’s collapse. “What it is clear is that we cannot change our shared past but we can choose our shared future and the future must be European. European in the sense that we will respect differences, but this would be the future without divisions, where everybody feels at home,” Kos said. “It is very clear to me that we are not asking to forget differences. We are building, and this is my important task, a Europe where actually differences will no longer be a reason to live apart,” she added.

articles.title: Second Trial of Kosovo’s Thaci, for Obstructing Justice, Nears End
articles.summary: Verdict looms on Tuesday in former President Hashim Thaci's second trial at The Hague, in which he is accused of interfering with witnesses in the earlier war-crimes case against him.
articles.body: This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp The second trial of former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci at The Hague is coming to an end, with the verdict to be announced on Tuesday. Thaci, who was also a wartime guerrilla leader, is being tried alongside four co-defendants for obstruction of justice. He is accused of interfering with witnesses in his war-crimes trial. The Kosovo Specialist Prosecutor’s Office in The Hague, in its closing statements on September 10, demanded six years’ prison for Thaci, claiming he told his co-defendants to instruct witnesses what to say while testifying in his war-crimes case. It sought “nine months of imprisonment for [Hajredin] Kuci; three years for [Fadil] Fazliu; three years for [Isni] Kilaj; three years for [Bashkim] Smakaj; and six years for Thaci,” prosecutor Joshua Hafetz said during the closing statements. The prosecution claimed that Thaci tried to exert influence over two former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters, Bislim Zyrapi and Rrustem Mustafa, who were testifying in his war-crimes case. The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence. In his testimony in 2023, former KLA area commander Mustafa claimed that the KLA zone commanders made the key operational decisions, not the General Staff. He said the KLA leaders, who included Thaci, did not have control over lower-ranking fighters – testimony that bolstered the defence’s case. Zyrapi, former chief of the KLA’s General Staff, gave his testimony in 2024. He also said the General Staff often was not informed of the actions of fighters in the operational zones and that, despite attempts, it had not been possible for the KLA to fully exercise control over its lower-level units, partly because of Serbian offensives. On September 16 this year, the Specialist Chambers sentenced Thaci to 25 years in prison for the war crimes of murder, arbitrary detention, torture and cruel treatment as a leader of the KLA during the Kosovo war from April 1998 to June 20, 1999. His co-defendants, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli, and Rexhep Selimi, were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years respectively. The defence is preparing to appeal the first-instance verdict. The September 16 verdict triggered protests in Kosovo and in Europe by Albanian diaspora members and supporters of the KLA. Kosovo’s parliament on October 6 voted to amend the law on the Specialist Chambers to curb its powers. The law has been returned to parliament for review by the President, however . The EU and the UK have warned Kosovo MPs not to vote for the law change without consultations with the international community, as the court was established via an international agreement. The Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

articles.title: Serbia’s Post-Election Wave of Arrests Raises Hopes, But Also Questions
articles.summary: A flurry of arrests after Aleksandar Vucic’s party was defeated in Serbia’s elections has encouraged hopes that real institutional change could be coming, but has also sparked fresh questions about past failures under the outgoing government.
articles.body: After two days of celebrations in the wake of the momentous elections that ended the 14-year rule of the Serbian Progressive Party last month, police arrested Radivoje Stojkovic, the director of the Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj High School in the northern city of Novi Sad. During the course of nearly two years of student-led anti-government protests, which began in Novi Sad in 2024, school director Stojkovic had become one of the symbols of the pressures exerted on teachers who went on strike to express their support for their students and their own dissatisfaction. Stojkovic was detained on October 28 because he refused to enforce four court rulings and reinstate four teachers who had been ousted after they supported the student protests. The high school headed by Stojkovic is well-known in Serbia as the source of a key piece of protest lore. It was here that anti-protest graffiti reading "Caci u skolu" ("Pupils, go back to school") appeared. Because it was written with a spelling mistake, the term "caci" became a nickname for all supporters of the Serbian Progressive Party and its long-dominant figurehead, Aleksandar Vucic. Because of this, Stojkovic's arrest served as a symbolic beginning to what has followed since October 28: almost daily arrests of people close to the outgoing Progressive Party-led government, who are now being accused of abusing their positions, engaging in corruption or committing other illegal acts. articles.title: Kazakhstan considers new rules to flag risks in online games
articles.summary: The Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament, has proposed a bill that would introduce labeling requirements for online games, allow them to be checked and potentially blocked if they pose a threat. Digital platforms would also be required to introduce parental controls to restrict children’s ability to access or download games.
articles.body: The Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s parliament, has proposed a bill that would introduce labeling requirements for online games, allow them to be checked and potentially blocked if they pose a threat. Digital platforms would also be required to introduce parental controls to restrict children’s ability to access or download games. Notably, the bill is being discussed just days before the release of «Grand Theft Auto 6.» The criteria outlined in the bill include in-game purchases and chat functions. These provisions could also cover popular multiplayer games such as «Counter-Strike 2» and «Dota 2.» The proposal was discussed during Government Hour on Nov. 16, after Deputy Chair of the Kurultai Dinara Zakiyeva introduced the initiative. «It is envisaged that the safety of all digital and information products, including online games, will be ensured by introducing requirements for platforms to label and describe their digital risks, such as the ability to chat and in-game purchases. Furthermore, the proposal provides for a mechanism for mandatory verification by an authorized government body, monitoring for violations, and requiring the removal or blocking of information or digital products if a threat or risk associated with such a product, such as a game, is identified,» Zakiyeva said. It has yet to be announced which government body will be responsible for checking the games, what fines platforms could face and what criteria will be used to assess risks. Platform owners will be held responsible for all identified violations. Meanwhile, players who preordered a digital copy of “Grand Theft Auto 6» could begin preloading the game on Nov. 10, while its official release is scheduled for Nov. 19. The bill is unlikely to be passed before then. After the government issues its assessment, it will have to be reviewed by the Kurultai. It remains unclear how the regulations would apply to international digital stores and games that have already been released. The criteria outlined in the bill could also apply to other multiplayer games. «Counter-Strike 2» and «Dota 2» both feature in-game chat and purchases, exposing players to the risks that platforms would be required to flag. However, it remains unclear whether these provisions would cover such games or how they would apply to game developers and distribution platforms like Steam. Valve, the company behind both games and Steam, is also one of the largest foreign taxpayers in Kazakhstan .

articles.body: Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the production, sale and free distribution of polyethylene bags will be prohibited in Kyrgyzstan, except for those that meet new requirements. President Sadyr Japarov said this during a meeting with residents of the Ton and Jeti-Oguz districts, Kaktus.media reported. Kyrgyzstan began restricting the use of polyethylene bags in 2023. At the time, the Issyk-Kul region restricted their sale to protect the resort area’s environment. However, local shops eventually returned to using plastic bags. An entrepreneur from the village of Bokonbaevo, who launched a paper bag production business two months ago, told Japarov about the development. «Everyone complied with the ban for the first and second years, but then, I don’t know, maybe people got distracted by the World Nomad Games or for some other reason, everyone switched to plastic bags,» the businessman said. Japarov responded that starting in January, the ban would apply nationwide. The president also pledged to meet with the entrepreneur in person and help him develop his business. Kyrgyzstan will also ban plastic coffee pods, egg packaging, plastic mesh packaging for food products and nonrecyclable single-use tableware. Meanwhile, plastic bottles and food containers will remain available for sale. In July 2025, they were removed from the list of prohibited items. Separately, Kazakhstan is also considering a ban on single-use tableware , including plastic cups, plates and cutlery, while helping develop an international agreement that would impose strict restrictions on such products, Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Zhomart Aliyev said.

articles.title: Putin and Xi Jinping to hold Russian-Chinese talks on November 18 — Kremlin aide
articles.summary: Yury Ushakov noted that the meeting between the leaders of the two countries in Shenzhen would mark their fifth contact since the beginning of this year
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 16. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold bilateral talks on November 18 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters. "After his speech [at the APEC CEO Summit], our president will move on to the next part of this APEC summit, which is a very important bilateral segment. Russian-Chinese talks will begin, involving, naturally, Putin, Xi Jinping, and the respective delegations from both countries," the Kremlin official stated. Ushakov noted that the meeting between the leaders of the two countries in Shenzhen marks their fifth contact since the beginning of this year. "Typically, the leaders begin the year with a bilateral videoconference or a phone call. This was followed by an official visit to Beijing on May 20, where a meeting was held. They also met during the SCO summit in Bishkek, and held talks during the BRICS summit in New Delhi as well," he recounted.

articles.title: Crimean Bridge attack geared to disrupt peace talks — Russian lawmaker
articles.summary: "The Ukrainian aggressor’s attacks can be interpreted as yet again spitting on the large-scale peacemaking efforts by the American side, which is trying to stop bloodshed," Mikhail Sheremet stated
articles.body: SIMFEROPOL, November 16. /TASS/. By striking the Crimean Bridge, Ukraine is seeking to derail peace talks spearheaded by the United States, a Russian lawmaker told TASS. Crimea’s head Sergey Aksyonov said earlier that Ukrainian troops had struck the Crimean Bridge, temporarily halting motor traffic. "The Ukrainian aggressor’s aggressive attacks can be interpreted as yet again spitting on the large-scale peacemaking efforts by the American side, which is trying to stop bloodshed, and the Kiev junta’s open refusal from peaceful dialogue," said Mikhail Sheremet, a member of the Russian State Duma, or lower house of parliament, from Crimea. "This lunatic Zelensky wants to continue the war while staying in his comfortable hideout abroad, as the infrastructure of his dying country is being destroyed everywhere," he added. Another State Duma member from Crimea, Leonid Ivlev, also told TASS that he thinks that Zelensky doesn’t want to end the conflict and uses any steps toward peace agreements only as an opportunity to stockpile weapons and deliver more strikes on Russia. The current Kiev regime, acting on the instructions of its Western European sponsors, is ready to commit ever greater atrocities, the lawmaker stated. "And the Crimean Bridge stood, stands, and will continue to stand, despite the Ukrainian army’s attempts to strike it and the blather of talkative bloggers who, with a cynical eye, are calculating mythical damage percentages," he added.

articles.title: Russia, UAE hold talks on cooperation in military-technical, space, banking sectors
articles.summary: A Memorandum of Understanding between the office of Russia’s Security Council and the Supreme Council for National Security of the UAE will serve to deepen cooperation
articles.body: ABU DHABI /UAE/, November 16. /TASS/. Representatives from Russia and the UAE held separate talks on cooperation in the military-technical, space, and banking sectors, Russian Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu said at a meeting with Secretary-General of the UAE’s Supreme Council for National Security Ali Al Shamsi. "The delegation includes high-ranking representatives from ministries and agencies responsible for cooperation with the UAE. They held separate talks with their Emirati counterparts in the following areas: military-technical cooperation, interaction in the areas of justice and law enforcement, interbank cooperation, space exploration, and the peaceful use of atomic energy," Shoigu said. A Memorandum of Understanding between the office of Russia’s Security Council and the Supreme Council for National Security of the UAE will serve to deepen cooperation, he added. The parties have signed the relevant document.

articles.title: West can't take down Russia's hypersonic missiles as claimed — expert
articles.summary: According to Alexander Stepanov, Ukraine, which is entirely dependent on foreign military technology, is currently incapable of independently producing electronic warfare systems designed to intercept ballistic weapons
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 16. /TASS/. Claims that Russia’s Oreshnik hypersonic missiles can be intercepted using electronic warfare (EW) systems are a myth that the Western military-industrial complex is trying to pass off as reality in order to save face after the total failure of missile defense systems in the Middle East, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA)," told TASS, commenting on a New York Times article about the Lima Quant system. "Intercepting hypersonic weapons is a cherished myth of the Western military-industrial complex. They are promoting this narrative through their Ukrainian proxies, from whose positions they are, of course, testing various systems--but so far, as we can see, with little success," the expert said. According to him, Ukraine, which is entirely dependent on foreign military technology, is currently incapable of independently producing electronic warfare systems designed to intercept ballistic weapons. "If we’re to say that they are de facto incapable of countering the Kinzhal and Tsirkon missiles, then there’s no point in even discussing the Oreshnik, which surpasses them in every respect, including speed," Stepanov noted. The expert explained why it's so hard to take down a hypersonic missile. "This is due to the formation of a plasma cloud through which the warhead travels during the terminal phase, which effectively blocks any potential effect of electronic countermeasures," he said. Furthermore, the Oreshnik flies according to a flight plan with target designation that does not require corrections during the terminal phase, therefore, any interference with its navigation equipment would also be ineffective. "These claims are unfounded, technologically unjustified, and physically and materially unachievable at the current stage of development of Western defense industry technology," Stepanov emphasized. He added that the Kiev-25 production facility, where the Lima Quant device was stored, was recently shut down. "It is quite possible that tests of relevant Western solutions were conducted from a position controlled by the Kiev regime--nothing more. And, as we understand it, they were unable to prove their effectiveness in this theater of operations," the expert concluded. Earlier, a Ukrainian Night Watch territorial defense unit commander, with the call sign Alchemist, stated in an interview with The New York Times that the Lima Quant electronic warfare system diverted two Russian Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles from their targets during an attack on the Kiev Region on May 24, 2026. According to Alchemist, one missile struck garages in the Kiev Region, while the second disintegrated in flight, with its debris falling on territory under Russian control. Russian President Vladimir Putin, commenting on the situation, said that the Russian Armed Forces had struck targets where it was convenient to see the results. Russia struck a "shed" in Ukraine with an Oreshnik missile to observe how "the independently targetable warheads spread," the president said.

The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples. Qatar’ s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on the Qatar news agency (QNA): double quotation mark The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.
